clinicalPearls: A myeloproliferative neoplasm with clonal proliferation of eosinophils causing persistent marked eosinophilia
Organ damage from eosinophil infiltration and granule release can affect the heart, skin, lungs, gut and nervous system
It must be distinguished from reactive eosinophilia and from idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome
Clonality is shown by cytogenetic or molecular abnormalities or an increase in blasts
Cases with rearrangements of PDGFRA, PDGFRB or FGFR1 are classified separately and are important because PDGFR-driven disease responds dramatically to tyrosine kinase inhibitors
Endomyocardial fibrosis is a serious complication of sustained eosinophilia
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic eosinophilic leukaemia is a clonal stem cell neoplasm in which acquired genetic lesions drive autonomous eosinophil production. In an important subset, fusion genes involving PDGFRA (such as FIP1L1-PDGFRA), PDGFRB or FGFR1 constitutively activate tyrosine kinase signalling; these are now categorised as a distinct group of myeloid neoplasms with eosinophilia. The expanded eosinophils release granule proteins that damage tissues, with the heart particularly vulnerable to eosinophilic myocarditis and progressive endomyocardial fibrosis.
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and film quantifying eosinophilia
Molecular testing for PDGFRA, PDGFRB and FGFR1 rearrangements
Exclusion of reactive causes including parasites and allergy
Cardiac assessment (troponin, echocardiography) for eosinophilic heart disease
redFlags: Very high eosinophil counts with organ dysfunction
reference.prognosis: Prognosis varies with the genetic subtype; PDGFR-rearranged disease usually responds very well to tyrosine kinase inhibitors, whereas other forms depend on organ damage and risk of leukaemic progression.
pitfalls: Failing to test for PDGFR rearrangements, missing a highly treatable subtype
Attributing clonal eosinophilia to a reactive cause
Confusing it with idiopathic hypereosinophilic syndrome
management: Tyrosine kinase inhibition with imatinib as definitive therapy for PDGFRA- and PDGFRB-rearranged disease, which responds dramatically
Corticosteroids for urgent control of eosinophil-mediated organ damage while molecular results are pending, particularly with cardiac involvement
Cytoreduction with hydroxycarbamide and interferon-alfa for non-PDGFR clonal disease, with allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation for aggressive or FGFR1-rearranged disease
Cardiac surveillance with troponin and echocardiography, with anticoagulation and heart-failure therapy for eosinophilic endomyocardial disease and thrombosis
Exclusion of reactive eosinophilia and monitoring for leukaemic blast-phase progression
Haematology specialist management with molecular monitoring of treatment response
